title: LLM-as-a-tutor in EFL Writing Education: Focusing on Evaluation of Student-LLM Interaction
extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language models (LLMs) can function as tutors in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing education, with a particular focus on how to evaluate student-LLM interaction in pedagogically meaningful ways. The authors argue that standard LLM evaluation metrics, which mainly assess output quality, are insufficient for educational settings because writing feedback must also be judged in terms of its usefulness for learning, its pedagogical characteristics, and its effects on students’ understanding and confidence.

The study investigates an LLM-as-a-tutor approach for generating essay feedback using GPT-3.5-turbo. The authors first conduct exploratory interviews with six EFL learners and written interviews with three instructors to identify feedback needs. They then compare standard prompting with a score-based prompting method, where rubric-based essay scores (content, organization, language) from an automated essay scoring model are supplied to the LLM to guide feedback generation. To evaluate this, 21 English education experts rate the quality and characteristics of the generated feedback, and 33 EFL learners receive score-based feedback through the RECIPE platform as part of their writing coursework and report on their learning outcomes.

The population is primarily undergraduate EFL learners at KAIST and instructors/English education experts in South Korea. The educational context is EFL writing courses in a college setting, where students write essays independently and receive AI-generated feedback integrated into coursework. The study involves both student and teacher perspectives: teachers assess output quality and feedback characteristics, while students assess perceived essay improvement and understanding of rubric criteria after revising with LLM feedback.

The main conclusion is that score-based prompting produces more pedagogically appropriate feedback than standard prompting. Experts judged it as more accurate, relevant, helpful, and more aligned with EFL learners’ needs by being more direct, constructive, and specific. Most teacher annotators preferred score-based feedback. Students also reported improved confidence in essay quality and better understanding of rubric criteria, along with high satisfaction with the feedback. At the same time, the paper notes a key limitation: because ChatGPT is used as a black-box model, the system lacks transparency and explainability in how feedback is generated.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family conversational large language model used here as an English writing tutor that generates rubric-based essay feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo, normalized to ChatGPT) as an EFL writing tutor that provides feedback on student essays under standard prompting and score-based prompting, with teacher/expert evaluation of feedback quality/characteristics and student self-reported learning outcomes after receiving the feedback through the RECIPE platform.

findings.finding_summary: In an initial evaluation of standard-prompted ChatGPT feedback, 21 English education experts rated the feedback as highly positive (mean=5.93/7) but not very direct (mean=3.72/7), and judged it relatively unhelpful (mean helpfulness=3.41/7). The authors interpret this as a limitation for EFL writing support because learners preferred more direct, critical feedback.
findings.measure: Expert 7-point Likert ratings of positivity, directness, and helpfulness of ChatGPT-generated essay feedback

findings.finding_summary: Compared with standard prompting, score-based prompting with ChatGPT produced feedback that outperformed standard prompting on accuracy, relevance, and helpfulness across all rubrics, with statistical significance at p<0.05 by paired t-test. Teachers also preferred the score-based feedback in 74.38% of cases versus 12.50% for standard prompting, with 13.12% reporting no difference; this preference difference was significant at p<0.05 (Chi-squared), with Fleiss' Kappa=0.22.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of feedback quality and preference between standard vs score-based ChatGPT feedback
findings.effect_size: 74.38% preferred score-based vs 12.50% standard; Fleiss' Kappa=0.22

findings.finding_summary: Score-based prompting made ChatGPT feedback more negative, straightforward, direct, and extensive than standard prompting across all rubrics. Despite being judged more extensive, the score-based feedback was also more concise in form, using fewer tokens on average (70.46 vs. 79.19) and fewer sentences (4.20 vs. 5.04).
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of feedback characteristics plus token and sentence counts for generated feedback

findings.finding_summary: Among 33 EFL learners who received score-based ChatGPT feedback as part of coursework, students reported significant improvement in confidence about essay quality and understanding of the writing rubrics, with significance tested using the Wilcoxon test at p<0.05. Students also reported high satisfaction, rating feedback quality at 6.0/7 and feedback characteristics at 6.03/7.
findings.measure: Student self-reported confidence, rubric understanding, and satisfaction questionnaire after revising with ChatGPT feedback

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods study with expert ratings and student self-reports, but it is not an RCT or strong quasi-experimental design. Outcomes rely largely on perceived helpfulness, preferences, and self-reported learning rather than externally validated achievement gains.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant improvements in feedback ratings and student perceptions, but does not provide standardized effect sizes or objective pre-post writing performance gains. Impact appears promising but remains unclear in magnitude.
